name: Fairchild 500-element linear CCD
summary: Fairchild demonstrated a 500-element linear CCD design by May 1972 and offered the CCD101 for prototyping in May 1973.
description: Fairchild’s 500-element linear sensor captures light in a row of photosensitive elements, then shifts the charge through two shielded registers for sequential readout. Its buried channel reduces loss of charge to traps at the silicon–oxide interface.

impact.note: Solid-state electronic imaging spread through cameras, scanners and astronomy in many societies and founded digital imaging, later largely displaced by CMOS sensors.

events.statement: Electronics reported and illustrated a working 500-element buried-channel linear sensor built at Fairchild’s Palo Alto research center.
events.scope: Precommercial design that Fairchild planned to market as its first commercial 500-element CCD.
events.caveats: The 1972 prototype was reported without a model name. The prototype-to-product sequence is traced through Fairchild’s reported launch plan. The original prototype’s physical identity and any design revisions remain unresolved.

links.statement: Fairchild used the Bell Labs concept of clocked charge transfer to build a linear imager. Fairchild staff learned about Bell’s CCD work through direct contact and recruited one of its early experimenters.
links.caveats: The relation concerns the overall CCD readout principle and program. The origin of Fairchild’s specific buried-channel structure is less certain.

evidence.locator: Interview exchange before Buried channel charge-coupled devices, and the section itself
evidence.supports: The Fairchild director recalls the Bell Labs discussion and visit before establishing the Fairchild program and recruiting Amelio.

evidence.locator: Manufacturing and picture phone market; Bell stops CCD research
evidence.supports: Smith corroborates Amelio’s involvement in the early Bell experiment, move to Fairchild and role in its CCD effort.
Fairchild’s working device reads out light-generated charge with the clocked charge-transfer principle.

links.statement: Fairchild’s 500-element imager and the Bell Labs buried-channel design both placed the charge-transfer path inside the silicon, reducing loss to traps at the silicon–oxide boundary.
links.caveats: Early recalled conceiving a buried-channel design before learning of Bell’s earlier work. Kim’s later citation establishes awareness by 1973. A direct transfer of the specific Bell design into the CCD101 is unresolved.

evidence.supports: Bell Labs describes the subsurface storage and transport path and its effect on interface trapping.
